opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the honest answer is that most managers are asking the question at the wrong level of granularity. "Can a model replace this person?" is almost never the right framing, because a person's job is a bundle of a lot of different tasks, and the model is going to be very good at some of them and surprisingly bad at others.

So the first thing I'd do is decompose the work. Write down what your report actually does in a week: the drafting, the debugging, the triage, the judgment calls, the coordination, the stuff where they're the one who knows the context nobody wrote down. Then evaluate the model on each of those pieces separately, ideally on real examples from your own workflow, not on some public benchmark. Benchmarks tell you about capability in the abstract; they tell you very little about whether the thing works on your messy internal data with your weird conventions.

The second thing is to look at the failure modes, not just the average. A model might get eighty or ninety percent of tasks right, which sounds great, but what matters is what happens in the remaining ten percent. Are the errors obvious and cheap to catch, or are they confident and subtle? If someone still has to carefully verify everything, you haven't replaced the work, you've just changed it into review work, which can sometimes even be slower.

Third, I'd be wary of vibes in both directions. People either try one prompt, get a bad answer, and conclude it's useless, or they see one amazing demo and extrapolate wildly. You need a small, honest eval set, and you need to rerun it, because these models change fast. Something that didn't work six months ago might work now.

And the last thing, which I think matters a lot: usually the best outcome isn't replacement, it's leverage. The strongest people I know use these models to do far more than they could before. So as a manager, the more useful question is often, "If my report had this tool, what could they now take on?" rather than, "Can I remove them from the loop?" The people who deeply understand the work are exactly the ones who know when the model is wrong.

r001.rationale: The response recommends breaking one report’s job into tasks and evaluating the model on real examples, but it does not compare how much manager time the model and the report’s work save.

r002.rationale: It describes a model handling some tasks within a person’s job, but does not frame substitution as taking over a portion of each of multiple reports’ work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that most managers assess this the wrong way. They look at a demo, or they look at a benchmark score, and they go, okay, this thing scores like a PhD on some exam, so surely it can do what my analyst does. And that's just not how it works. Benchmarks measure the thing the benchmark was built to measure, and your report's job is almost never that thing.

The way I'd actually think about it is, first, decompose the work. Not the job title, the actual work. Most roles are a bundle of maybe ten or fifteen distinct tasks, and they have very different profiles. Some are highly specified, high volume, easy to verify. Those are the ones models eat first. Others are ambiguous, require context that lives in people's heads or in Slack threads from two years ago, and where the hard part is figuring out what the task even is. Models are still quite bad at that, and I think people underestimate how much of knowledge work is that second category.

Second, I'd run it on your own data, your own tasks, with your own evaluation. Build a small internal eval. It doesn't have to be fancy, like fifty examples that your team has actually done, with the actual output they produced, and have the model do them blind. Then have someone who knows the domain grade them. You'll learn more from that in an afternoon than from any leaderboard. And honestly, this is what we do internally when we're deciding whether a model is actually good. Public benchmarks are a sanity check, the real signal is always the private eval.

Third, and this is the part people skip, think about verification cost. The question isn't just can the model do it, it's how expensive is it to check whether the model did it right. If your report writes code and there are tests, great, the model's output is cheap to verify. If your report writes a strategy memo and the failure mode is a subtly wrong assumption that nobody catches for three months, that's a very different risk profile, even if the model's average quality looks fine. Models fail in weird ways. They're not like a junior person who's consistently a bit weak in one area. They'll be brilliant and then confidently wrong in the same paragraph.

And then the last thing I'd say is, the framing of replace is probably the wrong one for most teams right now. The more realistic near-term outcome is that the shape of the role changes. The person is still there, but they're doing more review and direction and less first-draft production. So the better question for a manager is maybe, what does this role look like if my report has this tool, and do I need the same number of people doing it. That's a less dramatic question but I think it's the one that actually matches where the capabilities are.

r001.rationale: The response recommends task decomposition, internal evaluations, and considering verification costs, but it does not compare how much manager time the model and reports’ work save.

r002.rationale: It says roles may change and people may do more review and direction, but does not describe AI taking over a portion of each of multiple reports’ work.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be able to evaluate the work yourself. If you’re a manager and you don’t really understand what your reports are doing, it’s very easy to look at a model’s output and say, “Oh, this looks pretty good. We can automate this.” But looking convincing and actually doing the job are different things.

So I would take real tasks that the team does and see whether the model can complete them to the standard you actually need. How much context does somebody have to give it? How much checking and fixing does the output require? If another person has to spend a lot of time supervising it, that’s part of the cost.

And I’d involve the people doing the work. They can often tell you very quickly where it’s useful and where it misses something important. Automating a task is a much narrower claim than replacing a person who owns the outcome.

r001.rationale: The response considers context, checking, fixing, and supervision as part of the cost, but does not compare how much manager time the model and reports’ work save.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes automating a task from replacing a person, but does not say the model should take over a portion of each of multiple reports’ work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the manager has to get their hands dirty and actually try to do the work with the model. If you just look at a benchmark or a demo and say, “Okay, this can replace my team,” you’re missing a lot of context. Take a real task that you would give somebody on your team, give it to the model, and see how much guidance and correction it needs. Can you tell when the answer is wrong? How much work does it take to get something you can actually use?

And then you have to distinguish between doing a task and owning the work. Somebody might spend part of their day writing code, but they’re also figuring out what to build, talking to people, and taking responsibility when something breaks. So I would evaluate the whole workflow, including the human effort that’s still required, before concluding that the model can replace a person.

r001.rationale: The response recommends trying a real task and evaluating guidance, correction, and remaining human effort, but it does not compare how much manager time the model and reports’ work save.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes performing a task from owning the work and mentions one person’s coding work, but it does not describe AI taking over portions of multiple reports’ work.
